results.name: in_range_setsize_slope
results.description: OLS slope, across number of examples (2-4), of the yes rate for non-example targets lying between the smallest and largest example; observed below null means people become less willing to fill in the range as examples accumulate, whereas the model predicts more (or flatter) range filling.
results.code:
# name: in_range_setsize_slope
# description: OLS slope, across number of examples (2-4), of the yes rate for non-example targets lying between the smallest and largest example; observed below null means people become less willing to fill in the range as examples accumulate, whereas the model predicts more (or flatter) range filling.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce")
    n = s.notna().sum(axis=1).to_numpy().astype(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    mn = s.min(axis=1).to_numpy(); mx = s.max(axis=1).to_numpy()
    is_ex = s.eq(pd.Series(t, index=s.index), axis=0).any(axis=1).to_numpy()
    m = (n >= 2) & (t > mn) & (t < mx) & ~is_ex
    if m.sum() < 3:
        return 0.0
    x = n[m]; y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()[m]
    xc = x - x.mean(); den = (xc ** 2).sum()
    if den <= 0:
        return 0.0
    return float((xc * (y - y.mean())).sum() / den)

results.name: far_outside_range_yes_rate
results.description: Yes rate for targets more than 30 below the smallest or above the largest example; observed above null means people say yes to far-away numbers (lapses / broad rules) more than the model predicts, below means the model over-generalises far.
results.code:
# name: far_outside_range_yes_rate
# description: Yes rate for targets more than 30 below the smallest or above the largest example; observed above null means people say yes to far-away numbers (lapses / broad rules) more than the model predicts, below means the model over-generalises far.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce")
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    mn = s.min(axis=1).to_numpy(); mx = s.max(axis=1).to_numpy()
    far = (t < mn - 30) | (t > mx + 30)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    if far.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[far].mean())

results.name: first_vs_last_example_proximity
results.description: For sets of 2-4 examples, yes rate for non-example targets within 4 of the first-shown example (and not within 4 of the last) minus the same for the last-shown example; observed below null means the model's first-example (sticky guess) primacy is too strong / people weight later examples more.
results.code:
# name: first_vs_last_example_proximity
# description: For sets of 2-4 examples, yes rate for non-example targets within 4 of the first-shown example (and not within 4 of the last) minus the same for the last-shown example; observed below null means the model's first-example (sticky guess) primacy is too strong / people weight later examples more.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce")
    n = s.notna().sum(axis=1).to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    first = s.iloc[:, 0].to_numpy()
    last = s.ffill(axis=1).iloc[:, -1].to_numpy()
    is_ex = s.eq(pd.Series(t, index=s.index), axis=0).any(axis=1).to_numpy()
    nf = np.abs(t - first) <= 4
    nl = np.abs(t - last) <= 4
    base = (n >= 2) & (~is_ex)
    a = base & nf & ~nl
    b = base & nl & ~nf
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: even_parity_boost_outside_range
results.description: For sets of >=2 examples that are all even, yes rate for even targets outside the examples' range minus odd targets outside it; observed above null means people generalise an arithmetic parity/multiples rule beyond the range more than the model predicts (below: the model over-weights such rules).
results.code:
# name: even_parity_boost_outside_range
# description: For sets of >=2 examples that are all even, yes rate for even targets outside the examples' range minus odd targets outside it; observed above null means people generalise an arithmetic parity/multiples rule beyond the range more than the model predicts (below: the model over-weights such rules).
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce")
    n = s.notna().sum(axis=1).to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    ev = ((s % 2 == 0) | s.isna()).all(axis=1).to_numpy() & (n >= 2)
    mn = s.min(axis=1).to_numpy(); mx = s.max(axis=1).to_numpy()
    out = (t < mn) | (t > mx)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    a = ev & out & (t % 2 == 0); b = ev & out & (t % 2 == 1)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: participant_yes_rate_sd
results.description: SD across sessions (a new session starts at each trial_index==0) of the per-session yes rate; observed above null means individual differences in overall yes-bias that the single-parameter-set model underproduces.

results.name: lag1_response_dependence
results.description: P(yes | previous trial yes) minus P(yes | previous trial no) over consecutive trials of the same session (trial_index increments by 1); observed above null means responses perseverate across trials, which the trial-independent model underproduces.
results.code:
# name: lag1_response_dependence
# description: P(yes | previous trial yes) minus P(yes | previous trial no) over consecutive trials of the same session (trial_index increments by 1); observed above null means responses perseverate across trials, which the trial-independent model underproduces.
def test_statistic(df):
    ti = df["trial_index"].to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    ok = np.diff(ti) == 1
    prev = r[:-1][ok]
    cur = r[1:][ok]
    if (prev == 1).sum() == 0 or (prev == 0).sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(cur[prev == 1].mean() - cur[prev == 0].mean())

results.name: yes_rate_trial_slope
results.description: OLS slope of rating (1=yes) on trial_index rescaled to [0,1]; observed more negative than null means people say yes less often as the session goes on, a drift the stationary model does not produce.
results.code:
# name: yes_rate_trial_slope
# description: OLS slope of rating (1=yes) on trial_index rescaled to [0,1]; observed more negative than null means people say yes less often as the session goes on, a drift the stationary model does not produce.
def test_statistic(df):
    x = df["trial_index"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    x = x / max(x.max(), 1.0)
    xc = x - x.mean()
    den = (xc ** 2).sum()
    if den <= 0:
        return 0.0
    return float((xc * (y - y.mean())).sum() / den)

results.name: shared_last_digit_boost
results.description: For sets of >=2 examples all ending in the same digit, yes rate for targets outside the examples' range that end in that digit minus those that do not; observed above null means people generalise an "ends in d" rule more than the model (with its digit-rule discount) predicts.
results.code:
# name: shared_last_digit_boost
# description: For sets of >=2 examples all ending in the same digit, yes rate for targets outside the examples' range that end in that digit minus those that do not; observed above null means people generalise an "ends in d" rule more than the model (with its digit-rule discount) predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce")
    n = s.notna().sum(axis=1).to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    ld = s % 10
    same = (ld.nunique(axis=1).to_numpy() == 1) & (n >= 2)
    d0 = ld.iloc[:, 0].to_numpy()
    mn = s.min(axis=1).to_numpy(); mx = s.max(axis=1).to_numpy()
    out = (t < mn) | (t > mx)
    match = (t % 10) == d0
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    a = same & out & match; b = same & out & ~match
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())
